title: Structural adaptations for enhanced translation kinetics in evolved ribosomes.
data_url: https://www.rcsb.org/structure/11BQ (plus 11GG, 11FV, 11EL, 11DG; EMDB EMD-75605, 75676, 75668, 75650, 75634); code at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21078135

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Confirmed all five deposited structures exist and download (RCSB entry records: cryo-EM, 2.9-3.2 Angstrom, 52-53 polymer chains each, released Apr-May 2026). Downloaded and parsed two gzipped mmCIF coordinate files (11bq.cif.gz 3.59 MB, 11fv.cif.gz 3.26 MB; ~16 MB uncompressed, 137,310 and 141,317 atom records). Extracted the 16S ribosomal RNA chain from each: 1,542 nucleotides in 11BQ and 1,526 in 11FV, and confirmed all five reported EC-S3.5 mutations are actually present in the 11BQ coordinates (position 412=C, 852=A, 904=C, 1415=A, 1419=A). Fetched the Zenodo record: it is a Mozilla/MIT-licensed code repository of contact-map scripts, no data. Listed the GitHub repository contents. Fetched the companion paper (Liu et al., Nature Communications 2021, PMC8463689) full text and counted the variants it measured.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The luciferase (light-producing enzyme) activity measurements themselves, which appear only in figure panels with n=4 replicates and are not in any deposited file. Supplementary Tables S1-S4 (cryo-EM statistics, conformational class occupancies, per-residue Q-score and local-resolution changes) could not be retrieved: the Europe PMC supplementary-files endpoint timed out on both attempts, so supplement not retrievable. Map file sizes in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank were not confirmed.

a1_downloadable.note: All five structures download without login from RCSB (~3.3-3.7 MB gzipped mmCIF each); I opened two of them. Zenodo code is open, MIT licence.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL. The thing a model would predict, translational activity, is not a column in anything this paper deposited: the deposits are only atomic coordinates and density maps. Activity exists only as bar heights in figures here and in the companion 2021 paper's Source Data file, so the label would have to be assembled by hand across two papers.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are genuinely present, not referenced: I extracted the full 16S ribosomal RNA sequence (1,542 nucleotides) and 137,310 atom coordinates directly from the 11BQ file.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are stated where they exist: resolution in Angstroms, luminescence and optical density at 600 nm for the activity assay, Q-score (a dimensionless map-to-model fit score) for local quality.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL, decisively. Five ribosome structures, plus two engineered compensatory variants measured only by activity assay. The largest joinable variant-activity set anywhere is the companion paper's 67 evolved ribosomal RNA mutants (I read '61/67 mutants' and '49/53 mutants' in its text). Against the ~1,500-row regression threshold, or ~400 for classification, this is two orders of magnitude short.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~0.1 GB for all five coordinate files uncompressed; density maps not sized
a6_fits_laptop.note: Coordinates fit easily on 16 GB; the cryo-EM density maps were not measured and could be several GB each, but are not needed for a sequence/coordinate task.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The paper's claims match the files: all five EC-S3.5 mutations the paper reports (A412C, G852A, U904C, G1415A, G1419A) are present at those positions in the 11BQ coordinates I parsed.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAIL for the alternative per-nucleotide project. The only per-position quantity available at scale is the Q-score or local-resolution change, which is computed from the same cryo-EM map that supplies the structural input, so the label is derived from the features. The real physical label (luciferase activity) is measured per ribosome, so n=5, not per nucleotide.

existing_models.name: GARNET RNA generative language model (Nature Communications 2024, 'RNA language models predict mutations that improve RNA function')
existing_models.score_and_split: Not a performance benchmark: the authors used a graph neural network plus a triplet-tokenised RNA language model to nominate ribosomal RNA mutations, then validated a U-to-C change at position 2477 in helix 89 experimentally for thermostability of the E. coli 50S subunit.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Retrieved by search only; I did not read the discussion, so I cannot quote what they named unsolved.

existing_models.name: Riboformer (Nature Communications 2024)
existing_models.score_and_split: Transformer predicting ribosome density at codon resolution from messenger RNA sequence context; different task (predicts where ribosomes sit on a transcript, not how fast an engineered ribosome works).

existing_models.name: Translatomer (Nature Machine Intelligence 2024)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported 0.72-0.80 accuracy for de novo prediction of cell-type-specific ribosome profiling; again a transcript-level task, not ribosomal RNA variant effect.

backbone.name: RNA-FM or an RNA language model such as the GARNET-style triplet-token model
backbone.hardware: CPU, since there would be at most dozens of 1,500-nucleotide sequences to embed
backbone.licence: Varies by checkpoint; not checked because the project dies at Part A

integration.partner_dataset: Companion paper Liu et al., Nature Communications 2021 (PMC8463689) Source Data, which holds activity and host doubling time for ~67 evolved orthogonal ribosomal RNA mutants; also the Protein Data Bank's other E. coli 70S ribosome structures (7K00, 4YBB, 8G7R and similar)
integration.join_key: 16S ribosomal RNA variant name (EC-S3.5, PA-S3.3, VC-S4.4) and nucleotide position in E. coli numbering
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Which 16S ribosomal RNA sequence changes raise translation speed, and can local structural destabilisation predict that gain? -- a real question, but with roughly 67 measured variants in total it is a statistics problem, not a machine-learning one.

controls.positive_control: The paper supplies a strong biological positive control in principle: compensatory mutations (U1437C in PA-S3.3, U1444G in VC-S4.4) that restore normal base pairing drop activity back to wild-type, so any model of destabilisation-versus-activity must reproduce that direction.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling is meaningless at n=5.
controls.external_validation: No second independent source of orthogonal-ribosome activity measurements was found.

honest_claim_h3: With five structures and roughly 67 measured variants across three bacterial species, the only honest claim is a descriptive correlation within this one laboratory's evolution campaign -- 'in these ribosomes, more local destabilisation of helix 44 went with higher activity' -- which the paper already makes without a model.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use 16S ribosomal RNA sequence and structure to predict how fast an engineered ribosome makes protein.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example would be one engineered ribosome: its 16S ribosomal RNA sequence (about 1,540 nucleotides, which I extracted from the deposited coordinates) plus structural features such as base-pair geometry and local map quality. I verified five such examples exist here, and found at most ~67 in the companion 2021 paper.
plain_idea.predict: Translation output, measured as light produced by a luciferase reporter enzyme normalised to cell density, read on a plate reader with four replicates. That measurement is not in any deposited file; it appears only in figure panels.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Groups engineering ribosomes for non-natural amino acids (the Badran lab at Scripps, the Chin lab at Cambridge) would use a predictor to pick which rRNA mutations to build next, saving rounds of directed evolution. But with five to 67 labelled examples, nothing learned would generalise.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: predict orthogonal translation activity from 16S ribosomal RNA sequence plus cryo-EM-derived structural destabilisation features, training on the evolved and starting ribosomes from this paper joined to the ~67 variants in the companion 2021 paper. Also considered a per-nucleotide task (predict local structural change from sequence context), which fails because the only per-position label, the Q-score change, is computed from the same map that provides the input, and because five structures give five independent groups.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed beyond the two files I actually parsed: each gzipped mmCIF is ~3.5 MB and expands to ~16 MB of text, so parsing all five peaks around 2 GB in pandas; cross-validation time is null because with five to 67 examples there is no meaningful cross-validation.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the ribosomes that have both a sequence and a measured activity number. I did this: five structures in this paper, two further engineered variants with activity only, and ~67 mutants in the companion 2021 Nature Communications paper. That count kills it in ten minutes.

verdict_reason: Fails A5 on sample size and A2 on label availability. The deposits are five cryo-EM ribosome structures -- I opened two and confirmed the reported mutations are really in the coordinates, so the data is honest and high quality, just tiny. The quantity a model would predict, translational activity from a luciferase assay, is in no deposited file; it lives in figure panels here and in the companion 2021 paper's Source Data, which covers at most ~67 evolved ribosomal RNA mutants. The only per-position label available at scale is the Q-score change, which is computed from the same cryo-EM map that would supply the model's input features, so it also fails A8. Five independent ribosomes cannot support a model, and this is an excellent structural-biology paper rather than a machine-learning dataset.
